passage: I'm Alka, Jasleen's bench partner in Class 10. When the history tests came back, Jasleen had eighty-eight, the top mark. Mrs Dutta held up the paper and said, "Jasleen! She doesn't put her hand up any more, even when I can see she knows. Last week she said, "What's the point? She thinks I copied anyway." She handed in the next assignment half-done. I can't tell what's really going on inside her. But I remember her reading the chapter on the bus, twice, before that test.

passage: Farhan Chacha stirred his tea. "Naveen, you asked why I became a science teacher. At fifteen I got full marks in a chemistry test. My teacher said, in front of the class, 'Farhan? Full marks? Are you sure you didn't sit next to someone clever?' Everybody laughed. So did I. After that, something went out of me. I stopped raising my hand. I stopped doing the extra problems. If I didn't try, nobody could say I'd cheated, or that I'd failed. My marks sank, and that teacher nodded as if he'd been right all along. Only in Class 12, when a new teacher pinned my lab report on the board, did I start trying again. So now, when a quiet student surprises me, I never act surprised. I just say, 'Good work. Keep going.'"

qa.q: What did the new teacher in Class 12 do with Farhan's lab report?
qa.a: Pinned it on the board.

qa.q: Why did Farhan stop raising his hand after the chemistry test?
qa.a: He felt that if he didn't try, nobody could say he had cheated or failed; the teacher's doubt made effort feel risky.

qa.q: What choice does Farhan Chacha make now as a teacher, and why?
qa.a: When a quiet student surprises him he never acts surprised and just says 'Good work. Keep going', so no student feels doubted the way he did.

qa.q: What might have changed for Farhan if the first teacher had simply said 'Good work'?
qa.a: Farhan might have kept trying instead of losing years of effort before the Class 12 teacher restored his belief.

grounding: An uncle recalls how a teacher's disbelief at his full marks led him to stop trying as a teenager, until another teacher's belief brought him back.

passage:
In the Class 10 room of their Guwahati school, Urmila Ma'am handed back the maths tests. "Bhupen, forty-six out of fifty?" She held the paper up to the light as if checking it was his. "Which tuition are you going to? Or who were you sitting next to?"
The class laughed. Bhupen laughed too, a second late.
Over the next month he stopped putting his hand up. When a hard problem came, he wrote the first line and left the rest, so if he got it wrong no one could say much, and if he got it right no one would be surprised. His friend Dhiman noticed he had stopped staying back for the extra sums.
At home his mother asked why he was scrolling instead of solving. "No point," he said. "She thinks I copied anyway."

qa.q: What went wrong in the month after, and what could turn it around?
qa.a: He disengaged to avoid scrutiny; a teacher praising his effort, or his mother talking to Ma'am, could help him believe in his work again.

"You got an A in chemistry!" Rehana waved the report card.
"Mm." Mehak didn't look up from her phone.
"Mehak! That's huge!"
"Did you see what Iyer ma'am wrote? 'Unexpected improvement.' Unexpected."
"So? It's an improvement."
"It means she thinks I cheated. Or got lucky."
Rehana sat down. "Did she say that?"
"She didn't have to. She made the whole class clap like I was a miracle."
"Okay, that's annoying. But you studied. I saw you."
"Next term I'm not bothering. If I get a B, nobody's surprised. Nobody stares."
"So you'll get worse on purpose so she's right?"
Mehak finally looked up. "When you put it like that, it sounds stupid."
"It is. Show her it wasn't luck." Rehana nudged her. "I'll quiz you on Thursday."

qa.q: What is Mehak feeling about the A?
qa.a: Mehak feels hurt and embarrassed, sure the teacher sees her success as luck or cheating.

qa.q: How does Rehana help Mehak reconsider giving up?
qa.a: Rehana points out that getting worse on purpose would prove the teacher right, and offers practical support by quizzing her on Thursday.

I'm Jasleen, in Class 10. Last month I got 92 in chemistry. When the teacher handed back my paper, she said, "Oh! Jasleen, you got 92? Really?" in front of everyone.
My friend Nazia said, "She sounded shocked."
I tried to smile, but it hurt. Did she think I couldn't do it? I'd worked so hard.
After that, I stopped raising my hand. I didn't do the extra problems. If I didn't try so hard, then when I didn't do well, it wouldn't prove anything. I know that sounds strange.
Nazia noticed. "You used to love chemistry."
I shrugged. "Maybe I'm just not a chemistry person."
But I'm not sure that's true. I think I just got scared of her face.

qa.a: Jasleen got 92.

qa.a: Jasleen felt hurt and doubted, then scared of trying and failing under the teacher's low expectations.

qa.q: What could help Jasleen get back her love of chemistry?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult about the comment, and remembering that the 92 came from hard work, not luck.

Seema was referred because her English marks have dropped. She told me that her English teacher, Sabina Ma'am, often says things like, "Very good, Seema, I didn't expect that from you," when she does well.
Seema said, "It makes me feel like she thinks I'm stupid." She has started skipping homework, saying, "If I don't try, then it doesn't count."

Got my history project back today. A+. Baljeet Sir held it up and said, "Deepak did this? I'm amazed!" Everyone laughed.
I, Deepak, felt my face go hot. Why amazed? Because I sit at the back? Because I failed maths last year?
